s: “They hated me without a cause.”—John 15:25

It is generally understood that the quotation our Savior refers to here is to be found in Psalm 35:19, where David says, speaking of himself directly and of the Savior prophetically, “Do not let those who are my enemies rejoice over me, nor let those who hate me without a cause wink with the eye.”

Our Savior applies that to himself, and so he in effect really tells us that many of the Psalms are Messianic, or refer to the Messiah; and therefore Dr. Hawker was not wrong when he said he believed the Psalms referred to the Savior, though he may have carried the truth too far.
But it will be a good plan, when we read the Psalms, if we continually look at them as referring not so much to David as to the man of whom David was the type, Jesus Christ, David’s Lord.
No being was ever more lovely than the Savior; it would seem almost impossible not to have affection for him.
Certainly at first sight it would seem far harder to hate him than to love him.
And yet, lovable as he was—indeed, “altogether lovely”—no being met with hatred so early, and no creature ever endured such continual persecution as he had to suffer.

No sooner is he brought into the world than the sword of Herod is ready to cut him off, and the innocents of Bethlehem, by their dreadful massacre, gave a sad foretaste of the sufferings Christ would endure, and of the hatred that men would pour upon his devoted head.
From his first moment to the cross, except for the brief lull while he was a child, it seemed as if the whole world were in league against him, and all men sought to destroy him.

That hatred showed itself in different ways: sometimes in open deeds, as when they took him to the brow of the hill and would have thrown him down headlong, or when they picked up stones again to stone him because he said that Abraham longed to see his day, and saw it, and was glad.

At other times that hatred showed itself in words of slander, such as these: “He is a drunkard and a winebibber, a friend of tax collectors and sinners”; or in looks of contempt, as when they eyed him with suspicion because he ate with tax collectors and sinners and sat down at table with unwashed hands.
At other times that hatred lived entirely in their thoughts, and they thought within themselves, “This man blasphemes,” because he said, “Your sins are forgiven you.”

But at almost every moment there was hatred toward Christ; and when they took hold of him and would have made him king, and a shallow, fleeting flood of popular applause would have carried him on to an unsteady throne, even then there was a hidden hatred toward him, held down only by loaves and fishes, which needed only an equal quantity of loaves and fishes offered by the priests to develop itself into the cry of “Crucify him, crucify him!” instead of the shout of “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”
Men of every rank hated him.
Most men have to meet with some opposition; but then it is often the opposition of one class, and there are other classes who regard them with respect.
The demagogue who is admired by the poor must expect to be despised by the rich; and he who labors for the aristocracy naturally meets with the contempt of the many.

But here was a man who walked among the people, who loved them, who spoke to rich and poor as though they were (as indeed they are) on one level in his blessed sight; and yet all classes conspired to hate him: the priests decried him because he spoiled their dogmas; the nobles would put him to death because he spoke of being a king; while the poor, for reasons best known to themselves, though they admired his eloquence and would often have fallen prostrate in worship before him because of the wonderful deeds he did—even these, led by men who ought to have guided them better, conspired to put him to death, and to complete their guilt by nailing him to the tree, and then, wagging their heads, told him that if he could build a temple in three days, he should save himself and come down from the cross.
Christ was the hated one, the slandered and scorned; he was “despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief.”

Now this morning we will try, first, to justify the Savior’s statement that he was hated without a cause; secondly, to dwell on the sin of men—that men hated him without a cause; and in the third place, to give a lesson or two to Christ’s own people, which they may well learn from the fact that their Savior was hated without a cause.
I. First, then, beloved, let us JUSTIFY WHAT THE SAVIOR SAID: “They hated me without a cause.”
And we note that, apart from the consideration of man’s sinfulness and Christ’s purity, there is certainly no cause whatever to be found why the world should have hated him.
First, let us consider Christ in his person.
Was there anything in Christ’s person as a man, when he lived in this world, which naturally tended to make anyone hate him?
Let us note that there was an absence of almost everything that stirs up hatred between one man and another.
In the first place, there was no great rank in Christ to stir up envy.

It is a well-known fact that, however good a man may be, if he is raised at all above his fellow creatures by riches or by title, then although men one by one will respect him, the many often speak against him, not so much for what he is as for his rank and his title.

It seems natural for men in the mass to despise nobles; each man individually thinks it a wonderfully fine thing to know a lord; but put men together, and they will despise lords and bishops and speak very lightly of principalities and powers.

Now Christ had none of the outward circumstances of rank: he had no chariot, no long sleeves, no elevation above his fellows; when he went out, there were no heralds to attend him, there was no pomp to do him honor.
In fact, one would think that Christ’s appearance would naturally have stirred up pity.
Instead of being raised above men, he did in some sense seem to be below them, for foxes had holes and the birds of the air had nests, but the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head.

Many a democrat has railed against the archbishop as he went past Lambeth Palace; but would he curse or despise him if he were told that the archbishop had nowhere to lay his head, but simply toiled for the truth’s sake and had no reward?

The envy naturally stirred up by rank, station and the like could not have operated in Christ’s case; there was nothing in his clothing to attract attention; it was the clothing of a peasant of Galilee—“of one piece, woven from the top throughout.”
Nor was there anything in his rank.
He might have been the son of an ancient royal family, but its royalty was apparently extinct, and he was known only as the son of the carpenter.
So in that sense they hated him “without a cause.”
Many people seem to have envy stirred up in them against those who exercise rule or government over them.
The very fact of a man having authority over me stirs up my evil passions, and I begin to look at him with suspicion because he is invested with that authority.

Some men naturally fall into line and obey simply because the rule has been made; principalities and powers are established, and they submit themselves for the Lord’s sake; but the many, especially in these republican times, seem to have a natural tendency to kick against authority simply because it is authority.

But if authorities and governments were changed every month, I believe that in some countries—in France, for instance—there would be as many revolutions under one government as under another; in fact, they hate all government there and wish to be without law, so that each man may do what is right in his own eyes.
But this did not operate in Christ’s case; he was not a king; he did not assume rule over the multitude.
It is true he was Lord over storms and seas; it is true he could command demons, and, if he pleased, men would have had to be his obedient servants; but he did not assume power over them.
He marshaled no armies, he proclaimed no laws, he made himself no great one in the land; the people did just as they liked, for all the authority he exercised over them.

In fact, instead of binding severe laws upon them, he seemed to loosen the rigidity of their system; for when the adulterous woman, who would otherwise have been put to death, was brought before him, he said, “Neither do I condemn you.”
And he relaxed, to a certain extent, the rigidity of the Sabbath ordinance, which was in some respects too burdensome, saying, “The Sabbath was made for man.”
Surely, then, they hated him “without a cause.”
Some men make others dislike them because they are proud.

I know some men whom I would have liked very well if the starch had been left out of them; I would really sympathize with them and admire them if they had the least degree of condescension, but they seem to walk about the world with such an air of pride!
They may not be proud—very likely they are not; but, as an old divine said, “When we see a fox’s tail sticking out of a hole, we naturally expect the fox is there.”
And somehow or other, the human mind cannot bear pride; we always kick against it.
But there was nothing of that in our Savior.
How humble he was!
Why, he stooped to anything.

He would wash his disciples’ feet; and when he walked about among men, there was no parade about him, as if he would say to them, “See my talent, see my power, see my rank, see my dignity; stand aside, I am greater than you.”
No, he takes his seat there.

There is Matthew the tax collector sitting beside him, and he does not think he is harmed by the tax collector, although he is the worst of sinners; and there is a harlot—he speaks to her; there is another with seven devils, and he casts the devils out of her; and another who has leprosy, and he even touches the leper, to show how humble he was and that there was nothing of pride about him.
Oh, if you could have seen the Savior! He was the very model of humility!
There were none of your forms of etiquette and politeness about him; he had that true politeness which makes itself affable to all men, because it is kind and loving to all.
There was no pride in the Savior, and so there was nothing to stir up men’s anger on that account.
Therefore they hated him “without a cause.”

There are others whom you cannot help disliking, because they are so snappish and waspish and angry; they look as if they were born on some terribly dark, stormy day, and as if no small quantity of vinegar had been used in the mixing of their bodies.

You could not sit long with them without feeling that you have to keep your tongue on a fairly tight chain; you must not talk freely, or there would be a quarrel, for they would make you an offender for a word.
You may say, “So-and-so is no doubt a good man; but really, that temper of his—I cannot bear it.”
And when a man stands prominently before the public with a nasty, sour disposition, one feels inclined to dislike him.
But there was nothing of this about our Savior.
“When he was reviled, he did not revile in return”; if men spat in his face, he said nothing to them; and when they struck him, he did not curse them; he sat still and bore their scorn.
He walked through the world with contempt and infamy constantly poured upon him; but “he did not answer a word”; he was never angry.

You cannot find, in reading the Savior’s life, that he spoke one angry word, except those words of holy wrath which he poured like scalding oil on the head of Pharisaic pride; then indeed his wrath did boil, but it was holy wrath.
With such a loving, kind, gentle spirit, one would have thought he would have gone through the world as easily as possible.
But, in spite of all that, they hated him.
Truly we can say, “They hated him without a cause.”
There is another set of people you can scarcely help disliking: they are selfish people.
Now, we know some persons who have a very excellent temper, who are extremely honest and upright, but they are so selfish!
When you are with them, you feel that they are friends to you only for what they can get out of you; and when you have served their purpose, they will simply lay you aside and try to find another.

In trying to do good, their good deed has an ulterior object, but somehow or other they are always found out; and no man in the world receives a greater share of public contempt than the man who lives a selfish life.
Among the most miserable men in the universe, kicked about the world like a football, is the selfish miser.
But in Christ there was nothing selfish; whatever he did, he did for others.

He had a marvelous power of working miracles, but he would not even turn a stone into bread for himself; he reserved his miraculous power for others; he did not seem to have a particle of self in his whole nature.
In fact, the description of his life might be written very briefly: “He saved others; himself he did not save.”
He walked about; he touched the poorest, the lowliest, and those who were most sick; he did not care what men might say of him; he seemed to have no regard for fame, or dignity, or ease, or honor.
Neither his bodily nor his mental comforts were in the least regarded by him.
Self-sacrifice was the life of Christ; but he did it with such ease that it seemed no sacrifice.

Ah, beloved, in that sense they certainly hated Christ without a cause; for there was nothing in Christ to stir up their hatred—in fact, there was everything, on the other hand, to bind the whole world to love and revere a character so eminently unselfish.

There is another sort of people I do not like, namely, the hypocritical; indeed, I think I could even live with the selfish man if I knew him to be selfish; but the hypocrite—do not let him come anywhere near where I am.
Let a public man be a hypocrite once, and the world will scarcely trust him again; they will hate him.
But Christ was free from any blame in this respect; and if they hated him, they did not hate him for that, for there never was a more unvarnished man than Christ.
He was called, you know, the child Jesus; because just as a child speaks his mind out and has no reserve and no craftiness, so it was with Jesus; he had no affectation, no deceit.
There was no change about him; he was “without variableness or shadow of turning.”
Whatever the world may say of Christ, they never said they believed he was a hypocrite; and among all the slanders they brought against him, they never disputed his sincerity.

Had they been able to show that he really had been deceiving them, they might have had some grounds for hating him; but he lived in the sunlight of sincerity and walked on the very mountaintop of continual observation.
He could not be a hypocrite, and men knew he could not; and yet men hated him.

Truly, my friends, if you survey the character of Christ in all its loveliness, in all its benevolence, in all its sincerity, in all its self-devotion, in all its intense eagerness to benefit man, you must indeed say, “They hated him without a cause.” There was nothing in Christ’s person to lead men to hate him.
In the next place, was there anything in Christ’s errand that could make people hate him?
If they had asked him, “For what reason have you come from heaven?” would there have been anything in his answer likely to stir up their indignation and hatred?
I think not. For what purpose did he come?

He came, first of all, to explain mysteries—to tell them what was meant by the sacrificial lamb, what the significance of the scapegoat was, what was intended by the ark, the bronze serpent, and the pot of manna; he came to tear the veil of the Holy of Holies and to show men secrets they had never seen before.
Should they have hated one who lifted the veil of mystery, made dark things light, and explained riddles?
Should they have hated him who taught them what Abraham longed to see, and what prophets and kings had longed to know but died without knowing?
Was there anything in that to make them hate him?
What else did he come for?
He came to earth to reclaim the wanderer; and is there anything in that which should make men hate Christ?

If he came to reform the drunkard, to reclaim the harlot, to gather in the tax collectors and sinners, and to bring prodigals back to their father’s house, surely that is an aim with which every philanthropist should agree; it is the very thing for which our governments are formed and fashioned, to bring men to a better state; and if Christ came for that purpose, was there anything in that to make men hate him?
For what else did he come?
He came to heal the diseases of the body; is that a legitimate object of hatred?
Shall I hate the physician who goes about healing all kinds of diseases free of charge?
Are deaf ears unstopped, are mouths opened, are the dead raised, are the blind made to see, and widows blessed with their sons?
Are these reasons why a man should be odious?
Surely he might well say, “For which of these works do you stone me?
If I have done good works, why do you speak against me?”
But none of these works were the cause of men’s hatred; they hated him without a cause.
And he came to earth to die, so that sinners might not die?
Was that a cause of hatred?
Ought I to hate the Savior because he came to quench the flames of hell for me?
Should I despise him who allowed his Father’s flaming sword to be quenched in his own lifeblood?
Shall I look with indignation on the substitute who takes my sin and griefs upon himself and carries my sorrows?
Shall I hate and despise the man who loved me better than he loved himself—who loved me so much that he visited the gloomy grave for my salvation?
Are these the causes of hatred?
Surely his errand was one that ought to have made us sing his praise forever and join the harps of angels in their rapturous songs.
“They hated me without a cause.”
But once more: was there anything in Christ’s doctrine that should have made us hate him?
No, we answer; there was nothing in his doctrine that should have stirred up men’s hatred.
Take the precepts in his teaching.
Did he not teach us to do to others as we would have them do to us?
Was he not also the exponent of everything lovely and honorable and of good report?
And was not his teaching the very essence of virtue, so that if virtue itself had written it, it could not have written such a perfect code of lovely morals and excellent virtues?
Was it the ethical part of his doctrines that men hated?
He taught that rich and poor must stand on one level; he taught that his gospel was not to be confined to one particular nation, but was to be gloriously expansive, so as to cover the world.
This, perhaps, was one principal reason for their hating him; but surely there was no justifiable cause for their indignation in this.
There was nothing in Christ to lead men to hate him.
“They hated him without a cause.”
II. And now, in the second place, I come to dwell on MAN’S SIN, that he should have hated the Savior without a cause.
Ah, beloved, I will not tell you of man’s adulteries and fornications and murders and poisonings and sodomies.

I will not tell you of man’s wars and bloodsheds and cruelties and rebellions; if I want to tell you man’s sin, I must tell you that man is a deicide—that he put his God to death and killed his Savior; and when I have told you that, I have given you the essence of all sin, the masterpiece of crime, the very pinnacle and climax of the terrifying pyramid of mortal guilt.
Man outdid himself when he put his Savior to death, and sin out-Heroded Herod when it killed the Lord of the universe, the lover of the human race, who came to earth to die.
Never does sin appear so exceedingly sinful as when we see it aimed at the person of Christ, whom it hated without a cause.
In every other case where man has hated goodness, there have always been some extenuating circumstances.

We never see goodness in this world without alloy; however great any man’s goodness may be, there is always some peg on which we may hang a criticism; however excellent a man may be, there is always some fault which may diminish our admiration or our love.
But in the Savior there was nothing of this.
There was nothing that could blot the picture; holiness stood out to the very life; there was holiness—only holiness.

Let a man hate Whitefield, one of the holiest men who ever lived, and he would tell you that he did not hate his goodness, but hated his ranting preaching and the extraordinary anecdotes he told; or he would pull out something that fell from his lips and hold it up to ridicule.
But in Christ’s case men could not do that; for though they sought false witnesses, yet their witnesses did not agree together.
There was nothing in him but holiness; and anyone with half an eye can see that the thing men hated was simply that Christ was perfect; they could not have hated him for anything else.
And so you see the abominable, detestable evil of the human heart—that man hates goodness simply because it is goodness.

It is not true that we Christian people are hated because of our infirmities; men make our infirmities a nail on which to hang their laughter; but if we were not Christians, they would not hate our infirmities.

They hold our inconsistencies up to ridicule; but I do not believe our inconsistencies are what they care about; we might be as inconsistent as all the rest of the world if we did not profess religion, or if they did not think we had any.

But because the Savior had no inconsistencies or infirmities, men were stripped of all their excuses for hating him, and it came out that man naturally hates goodness, because he is so evil that he cannot help detesting it.
And now let me appeal to every sinner present and ask him whether he ever had any cause for hating Christ.
But someone says, “I do not hate him; if he were to come to my house, I would love him very much.”
But it is very remarkable that Christ lives next door to you, in the person of poor Betty there.
She goes to such-and-such a chapel, and you say she is nothing but a poor canting Methodist.
Why don’t you like Betty?
She is one of Christ’s members, and “Inasmuch as you have done it to one of the least of these, you have done it to me.”
You say you do not hate Christ.
Now, look across the chapel.
Don’t you know a man, a member of this place, a very holy man, whom somehow or other you cannot bear, because he once told you of your faults?
Ah, sir, if you loved Christ, you would love his members.
What! Do you tell me you love my head, but you do not love my hands?
My dear fellow, you cannot cut my head off and leave me the same person.
If you love Christ the head, you must love his members.
But you say, “I do love his people.”
Very well, then you have passed from death to life, if you love the brothers.
But you say, “I am not sure that I am a changed character; still, I am not aware that there is any opposition in my heart to Christ and his gospel.”
You may not be aware of it, but it is your not being aware of it that makes your case all the sadder.
Perhaps if you knew it and wept over it, you would come to Christ; but since you do not know it and do not feel it, that is a proof of your hostility.
Now come! I must suppose you to be hostile to Christ unless you love him; for I know there are only two opinions of him.
You must either hate him or love him.
As for indifference with regard to Christ, it is simply a clear impossibility.
A man might as well say, “I am indifferent toward honesty.”
Why, then he is dishonest, is he not?
You are indifferent to Christ?
Then you hate him.
And why is it that you hate him?
Many a time you have been wooed by the gospel; you have resisted appeals, many of them; come now, for which of Christ’s works do you hate him?
Is there a persecutor here?
Sinner! For what do you hate Christ?
Do you curse him?
Tell me what he has done, that you should be angry with him.
Point to a single fault of his in his conduct toward you. Has Christ ever hurt you?
“Oh,” says one, “he has taken my wife and made her one of his children, and she has been baptized and goes to chapel, and I cannot bear that.”
Ah, sinner, is that why you hate Christ?
Would you have hated Christ if he had snatched your wife from the flames, if he had saved her from going down to death?
No, you would love him.
And he has saved your wife’s soul.
Ah! Even if he never saves you, if you love your wife, you will have cause enough to love him, when you think that he has been so good to you.
I tell you, if you hate Christ, you not only hate him without a cause, but you hate him when you have clear cause to love him.
Come, poor sinner, what have you gained by hating Christ?
You have stings of conscience.

Many a sinner, by hating Christ, has been locked up in jail, has a ragged coat, a diseased body, a nasty, filthy house with broken windows, a poor wife nearly beaten to death, and children who scamper out of the way as soon as father comes home.
What have you gained by hating Christ?
Oh, if you were to reckon up your gains, you would find that getting Christ would be a gain, but that hating him is a dead loss to you.

Now, if you hate Christ and Christ’s religion, I tell you that you hate Christ without a cause; and let me give you one solemn warning, which is this: if you keep on hating Christ until you die, you will not hurt Christ by it, but you will hurt yourself most terribly.
Oh, may God deliver you from being haters of Christ!
There is nothing to gain by it, but everything to lose by it.
For what cause do you hate Christ, sinner?
For what cause do you hate Christ, persecutor?
For what cause do you hate Christ, you carnal, ungodly men?
What do you hate Christ’s gospel for?
His ministers—what harm have they done you?
What harm can they do you, when they long to do you all the good in the world?
Why is it that you hate Christ?
Ah! It is only because you are so desperately set on mischief—because the poison of asps is under your lips, and your throat is an open grave.
Otherwise you would love Christ.
They hated him “without a cause.”
And now, Christian men, I must preach at you for just a moment.
Surely you have great reason to love Christ now, for you once hated him without a cause.
Did you ever treat a friend badly and not know it?
It has been the misfortune of most of us to do so at times.
We had some suspicion that a friend had done us an injury; we quarreled with him for weeks, and he had not done it at all.
All he had done was to warn us.
Ah! There are never tears like those we shed when we have wronged a friend.
And should we not weep when we have wronged the Savior?
Did he not come to my door one cold, damp night, and I shut my door against him?
Oh, I have done what I cannot undo; I have slighted my Lord, I have insulted my friend, I have heaped dishonor on him whom I admire.
Shall I not weep for him?
Oh, shall I not spend my very life for him? For my sins, my own treachery, spilled his blood.
Monuments—ah, monuments I will build, wherever I live, wherever I go.

I will pile up monuments of praise, so that his name may be spread; and wherever I wander, I will tell with many a tear what he did, and that I so long ill-treated him and so fearfully misunderstood him.
We hated him without a cause; therefore let us love him.

blocks.x: III. TWO LESSONS FOR THE SAINTS.

s: In the first place, if your Master was hated without a cause, do not expect to get off very easily in this world.
If your Master was subjected to all this contempt and all this pain, do you suppose you will always ride through this world in a chariot?
If you do, you will be greatly mistaken.
As your Master was persecuted, you must expect to be the same.
Some of you pity us when we are persecuted and despised.
Ah, save your pity; keep it for those of whom the world speaks well; keep it for those against whom the woe is pronounced.
“Woe to you when all men speak well of you.”
Save your pity for earth’s favorites; save your pity for this world’s lords, who are applauded by all men.

We do not ask for your pity; no, sirs, in all these things we rejoice, and “glory in tribulations also, knowing that the things which happen to us happen for the furtherance of the gospel”; and we count it all joy when we fall into all sorts of trials, for we rejoice that the name of Christ is known and his kingdom extended.
The other lesson is: take care, if the world does hate you, that it hates you without a cause.
If the world is going to oppose you, it is of no use making the world oppose you.
This world is bitter enough without my putting vinegar in it.
Some people seem to imagine the world will persecute them; so they put themselves into a fighting posture, as if they were inviting persecution.
Now, I do not see any good in doing that.
Do not try to make other people dislike you.
Really, the opposition some people meet with is not for righteousness’ sake, but for their own sin’s sake, or their own nasty temper’s sake.
Many a Christian lives in a household—a Christian servant girl, perhaps; she says she is persecuted for righteousness’ sake.
But she has a bad disposition; she sometimes speaks sharply, and then her mistress rebukes her.
That is not being persecuted for righteousness’ sake.
There is another, a merchant in the city, perhaps; he is not held in much esteem.
He says he is persecuted for righteousness’ sake; whereas it is because he did not keep a bargain some time ago.
Another man says he is persecuted for righteousness’ sake; but he goes about assuming authority over everybody, and now and then people turn around and reproach him.
See to it, Christian people, that if you are persecuted, it is for righteousness’ sake; for if you bring any persecution on yourself, you must bear it yourself.
The persecutions you bring on yourself by your own sins—Christ has nothing to do with them; they are chastisements on you.
They hated Christ without a cause; then do not fear to be hated.
They hated Christ without a cause; then do not court being hated, and give the world no cause for it.
And now may you who hate Christ love him! Oh, that he would bring himself to you now!
Oh, that he would show himself to you!
And then surely you must love him at once.
He who believes on the Lord Jesus will be sure to love him, and he who loves him shall be saved.
Oh, that God would give you faith, and give you love, for Christ Jesus’ sake! Amen.

“For this reason God also has highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things on earth, and things under the earth; and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”—Philippians 2:9-11
I almost regret this morning that I have ventured to occupy this pulpit, because I feel utterly unable to preach to you for your profit.

I had thought that the quiet and rest of the last two weeks had removed the effects of that terrible catastrophe; but on coming back to the same spot again, and especially standing here to address you, I feel something of those same painful emotions which nearly overwhelmed me before.
You will therefore excuse me this morning if I make no reference to that solemn event, or scarcely any.
I could not preach to you on a subject that was in the least connected with it.
I would be obliged to be silent if I were to call to mind that terrifying scene in the midst of which it was my solemn lot to stand.
God will overrule it, no doubt.

It may not have been so much by the malice of men, as some have claimed; it was perhaps simple wickedness—an intention to disturb a congregation; but certainly with no thought of committing so terrible a crime as the murder of those unfortunate people.
God forgive those who were the instigators of that horrible act!
They have my forgiveness from the depths of my soul.
It will not stop us, however; we are not in the least daunted by it.
I will preach there again yet; yes, and God will give us souls there, and Satan’s empire will tremble more than ever.
“God is with us; who is he that will be against us?”
The text I have selected is one that has comforted me and, in great measure, enabled me to come here today—the mere reflection on it had such power to comfort my depressed spirit.

It is this: “For this reason God also has highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things on earth, and things under the earth; and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”—Philippians 2:9-11.

I will not attempt to preach on this text; I will only make a few remarks that have occurred to my own mind; for I could not preach today; I have been utterly unable to study, but I thought that even a few words might be acceptable to you this morning, and I trust your loving hearts to excuse them.
O Spirit of God, magnify your strength in your servant’s weakness, and enable him to honor his Lord, even when his soul is cast down within him.
When the mind is intensely set on one object, however much it may be tossed to and fro by various calamities, it invariably returns to the place which it had chosen as its dwelling place.
You have noticed this in the case of David.
When the battle had been won by his warriors, they returned flushed with victory.

David’s mind had no doubt suffered much agitation in the meantime; he had dreaded the effects of victory and of defeat alike; but have you not noticed how his mind in one moment returned to the cherished object of his affections?
“Is the young man Absalom safe?” he said, as if nothing else that had happened mattered, if only his beloved son were secure!
So, beloved, it is with the Christian.

In the midst of calamities, whether they are the wreck of nations, the crash of empires, the upheaval of revolutions, or the scourge of war, the great question which he asks himself, and asks of others too, is this—Is Christ’s kingdom safe?
In his own personal afflictions his chief anxiety is—Will God be glorified, and will his honor be increased by it?

If it is so, he says, although I am only like smoking flax, yet if the sun is not dimmed I will rejoice; and though I am a bruised reed, if the pillars of the temple are unbroken, what does it matter that my reed is bruised?

He finds it sufficient consolation, in the midst of all the breaking in pieces which he endures, to think that Christ’s throne stands fast and firm, and that though the earth has rocked beneath his feet, yet Christ stands on a rock which can never be moved.
Some of these feelings, I think, have crossed our minds.

Amid much tumult and many rushings to and fro of troubled thoughts, our souls have returned to the cherished object of our desires, and we have found it no small consolation after all to say, “It does not matter what becomes of us: God has highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow.”
This text has given sweet consolation to every heir of heaven.
Allow me, very briefly, to give you its consolations.
To the true Christian there is much comfort in the very fact of Christ’s exaltation.
In the second place, there is no small degree of consolation in the reason for it.
“For this reason God also has highly exalted him”; that is, because of his previous humiliation.
And third, there is no small amount of truly divine comfort in the thought of the person who has exalted Christ.
“For this reason God also”—although men despise him and cast him down—“God also has highly exalted him.”
I. First, then, IN THE VERY FACT OF CHRIST’S EXALTATION THERE IS A VERY LARGE DEGREE OF COMFORT FOR EVERY TRUE CHRISTIAN.

Many of you who have no part or share in spiritual things, having no love for Christ nor any desire for his glory, will only laugh when I say that this is a very bottle of cordial to the lips of the weary Christian—that Christ, after all, is glorified.
To you it is no consolation, because you lack that condition of heart which makes this text sweet to the soul.
To you there is no joy in it; it does not stir your heart; it gives no sweetness to your life; for this very reason, that you are not joined to Christ’s cause, nor do you devoutly seek to honor him.
But the true Christian’s heart leaps for joy, even when cast down by various sorrows and temptations, at the remembrance that Christ is exalted, for in that he finds enough to cheer his own heart.
Note here, beloved, that the Christian has certain features in his character which make the exaltation of Christ a matter of great joy to him.
First, he has in his own opinion—and not in his own opinion only, but in reality—a relationship to Christ, and therefore he feels an interest in the success of his kinsman.

You have watched the father’s joy when, step by step, his boy has climbed to wealth or fame; you have seen the mother’s eye sparkle with delight when her daughter grew up to womanhood and burst forth in all the grandeur of beauty.
You have asked why they should feel such interest; and you have been told, because the boy was his, or the girl was hers.
They delighted in the advancement of their little ones because of their relationship.
Had there been no relationship, they might have been raised to be kings, emperors, or queens, and they would have felt but little delight.
But because of the fact of kinship, each step was invested with a deep and stirring interest.
Now, it is so with this Christian.
He feels that Jesus Christ, the glorified “Prince of the kings of the earth,” is his brother.

While he reveres him as God, he admires him as the man Christ, bone of his bone and flesh of his flesh, and he delights, in his calm and peaceful moments of communion with Jesus, to say to him, “O Lord, you are my brother.”
His song is, “My beloved is mine, and I am his.”
It is his joy to sing—

blocks.x: “In the blood with sinners one,”

s: Christ Jesus is; for he is a man, just as we are: and he is no less and no more man than we are, except only for sin.
Surely, when we feel we are related to Christ, his exaltation is the source of the greatest joy to our spirits; we take delight in it, seeing it is one of our family who is exalted.
It is the Elder Brother of the one great family of God in heaven and earth; it is the Brother to whom all of us are related.
There is also in the Christian not merely the feeling of relationship, but a feeling of unity in the cause.
He feels that when Christ is exalted, he himself is exalted in some degree, seeing he shares his desire to promote the great cause and honor of God in the world.

I have no doubt that every common soldier who stood by the side of the Duke of Wellington felt honored when the commander was applauded for the victory; for, he said, “I helped him, I assisted him; it was only a lowly part that I played; I only held my place in the ranks; I only endured the enemy’s fire; but now the victory is won.
I feel an honor in it, for I helped, in some degree, to win it.”
So the Christian, when he sees his Lord exalted, says, “It is the Captain who is exalted, and in his exaltation all his soldiers share.
Have I not stood by his side?

Little was the work I did, and poor the strength which I possessed to serve him; but still I helped in the labor”; and the commonest soldier in the spiritual ranks feels that he himself is in some degree exalted when he reads this—“For this reason God also has highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name”: a renown above every name—“that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow.”
Moreover, the Christian knows not only that there is this unity in purpose, but that there is a real union between Christ and all his people.
It is a doctrine of revelation seldom dwelt upon, but never thought of too much—the doctrine that Christ and his members are all one.
Do you not know, beloved, that every member of Christ’s church is a member of Christ himself?

We are “of his flesh and of his bones,” parts of his great mystical body; and when we read that our head is crowned, O rejoice, you members of his, his feet or his hands: though the crown is not on you, yet being on your Head, you share the glory, for you are one with him.
See Christ there, sitting at his Father’s right hand!
Believer! he is the pledge of your glorification; he is the guarantee of your acceptance; and, moreover, he is your representative.

The seat which Christ possesses in heaven he holds not only by his own right, as a person of the Godhead, but he holds it also as the representative of the whole church, for he is their forerunner, and he sits in glory as the representative of every one of them.
O rejoice, believer, when you see your Master raised from the tomb, when you behold him exalted up to heaven.

Then, when you see him climb the steps of light and sit on his lofty throne, where the sight of angels can scarcely reach him—when you hear the acclamations of a thousand seraphs—when you note the loud, pealing choral symphony of millions of the redeemed; think, when you see him crowned with light—think that you are exalted too in him, seeing that you are a part of himself.
Happy are you if you know this, not only in doctrine, but in sweet experience too.

Knit to Christ, wedded to him, grown into him, parts and portions of his very self, we throb with the heart of the body; when the head itself is glorified we share in the praise; we feel that his glorification bestows an honor on us.
Ah! beloved, have you ever felt that unity with Christ?
Have you ever felt a unity of desire with him?

If so, you will find this rich with comfort; but if not—if you do not know Christ—it will be a source of grief rather than a pleasure to you that he is exalted, for you will have to reflect that he is exalted to crush you, exalted to judge you and condemn you, exalted to sweep this earth of its sins, and cut the curse up by the roots, and you with it, unless you repent and turn to God with full purpose of heart.
There is yet another feeling which I think is extremely necessary for any very great enjoyment of this truth, that Christ is exalted.
It is a feeling of entire surrender of one’s whole being to the great work of seeking to honor him.
Oh! I have striven for that: how I wish to God I might attain it!
I have now concentrated all my prayers into one, and that one prayer is this, that I may die to self and live wholly for him.

It seems to me to be the highest stage of man—to have no wish, no thought, no desire but Christ—to feel that to die would be bliss, if it were for Christ—that to live in poverty and woe, and scorn, and contempt, and misery, would be sweet for Christ—to feel that it did not matter what became of oneself, so long as one’s Master was exalted—to feel that though, like a withered leaf, you are blown in the gale, you do not care at all where you are going, so long as you feel that the Master’s hand is guiding you according to his will.

Or rather to feel that though, like the diamond, you must be cut, you do not care how sharply you may be cut, so that you may be made fit to be a brilliant in his crown; that you care little what may be done to you, if only you may honor him.

If any of you have attained that sweet feeling of self-annihilation, you will look up to Christ as if he were the sun, and you will say of yourself, “O Lord, I see your beams; I feel myself to be not a beam from you—but darkness, swallowed up in your light.
The most I ask is that you would live in me, that the life I live in the flesh may not be my life, but your life in me, that I may say with emphasis, as Paul did, ‘For me to live is Christ.’”
A man who has attained this need never care what the opinion of this world is.
He may say, “Do you praise me?
Do you flatter me?
Take back your flatteries: I do not ask them at your hands; I sought to praise my Master; you have laid the praises at my door; go, lay them at his, and not at mine.
Do you scorn me?
Do you despise me?
Thrice happy am I to bear it.
If only you will not scorn and despise him!”

And if you will, yet know this, that he is beyond your scorn; and therefore strike the soldier for his Captain’s sake; yes, strike, strike; but the King you cannot touch—he is highly exalted—and though you think you have won the victory, you may have routed one soldier of the army, but the main body is triumphant.
One soldier seems to be struck down to the dust, but the Captain is coming on with his victorious cohorts, and will trample you, flushed with your false victory, beneath his conquering feet.
As long as there is a particle of selfishness remaining in us, it will spoil our sweet rejoicing in Christ; until we get rid of it, we will never feel constant joy.
I do think that the root of sorrow is self.
If we once got rid of that, sorrow would be sweet, sickness would be health, sadness would be joy, poverty would be wealth, as far as our feelings about them are concerned.
They might not be changed, but our feelings under them would be vastly different.
If you would seek happiness, seek it at the roots of your selfishness; cut up your selfishness, and you will be happy.

I have found that whenever I have yielded to the least joy, then I have been prepared to feel acutely the arrows of the enemy; but when I have said of the praises of men, “Yes, what are you? Worthless things!”—then I could also say of their contempt—“Come on! come on!

I will send you all where I sent the praises; you may go together and fight your battles with one another; but as for me, let your arrows rattle on my armor—they must not, and they shall not, reach my flesh.”
But if you give way to the one, you will give way to the other.
You must seek and learn to live wholly in Christ—to sorrow when you see Christ maligned and dishonored, to rejoice when you see him exalted—and then you will have constant cause for joy.

Sit down now, O reviled one, poor, despised, and tempted one; sit down, lift up your eyes, see him on his throne, and say within yourself, “Little though I am, I know I am united to him; he is my love, my life, my joy; I do not care what happens so long as it is written, ‘The Lord reigns.’”
II. Now, briefly, on the second point.
Here also is the very fountain and wellspring of joy, in THE REASON FOR CHRIST’S EXALTATION.
“For this reason God also has highly exalted him.”

Why? Because “he, being in the form of God, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but made himself of no reputation, and took upon himself the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men; and being found in outward form as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient to death, even the death of the cross.
For this reason God also has highly exalted him.”
This of course relates to the manhood of our Lord Jesus Christ.
As God, Christ needed no exaltation; he was higher than the highest, “God over all, blessed forever.”

But the symbols of his glory having been obscured for a while, having wrapped his Godhead in mortal flesh, his flesh with his Godhead ascended on high, and the man-God, Christ Jesus, who had stooped to shame, and sorrow, and degradation, was highly exalted, “far above all principalities and powers,” that he might reign as Prince Regent over all worlds, yes, over heaven itself.
Let us consider for a moment that depth of degradation to which Christ descended; and then, my beloved, it will give you joy to think that for that very reason his manhood was highly exalted.
Do you see that man—

blocks.x:
“The humble Man before his foes,
The weary Man and full of woes?”

s: Do you watch him as he speaks?
Note the marvelous eloquence which pours from his lips, and see how the crowds attend him?
But do you hear, in the distance, the growling of the thunders of calumny and scorn?
Listen to the words of his accusers.
They say he is “a gluttonous man and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners”; “he has a demon, and is mad.”
The whole vocabulary of abuse is exhausted in vilifying him.
He is slandered, abused, persecuted!
Stop! Do you think that he is cast down by this, degraded by this?
No, for this very reason: “God has highly exalted him.”
Mark the shame and spitting that have come upon the cheek of that man of sorrows over there!
See his hair plucked by cruel hands; notice how they torture him and how they mock him.
Do you think that this is all dishonorable to Christ?
It seems so; but listen to this: “He became obedient,” and therefore “God has highly exalted him.”

Ah! there is a marvelous connection between that shame and spitting and the bending of the knees of seraphs; there is a strange yet mystic link which unites the calumny and the slander with the choral harmonies of adoring angels.
The one was, as it were, the seed of the other.
Strange that it should be so, but the black, the bitter seed brought forth a sweet and glorious flower which blooms forever.
He suffered and he reigned; he stooped to conquer, and he conquered because he stooped, and was exalted because he conquered.
Consider him further still.
Do you see him in your imagination nailed to that cross!
O eyes! you are full of pity, with tears standing thick!
Oh! how I see the floods gushing down his cheeks!
Do you see his hands bleeding, and his feet too, gushing blood?
Behold him! The bulls of Bashan surround him, and the dogs are hounding him to death!
Hear him! “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?”
The earth starts up in fright.
A God is groaning on a cross!
What! Does this not dishonor Christ?
No; it honors him!
Each of the thorns becomes a brilliant in his diadem of glory; the nails are forged into his scepter, and his wounds clothe him with the purple of empire.
The treading of the winepress has stained his garments, but not with stains of scorn and dishonor.
The stains are embroideries on his royal robes forever.
The treading of that winepress has made his garments purple with the empire of a world; and he is the Master of a universe forever.
O Christian! sit down and consider that your Master did not mount from earth’s mountains into heaven, but from her valleys.
It was not from heights of bliss on earth that he strode to bliss eternal, but from depths of woe he mounted up to glory.
Oh! what a stride that was, when, at one mighty step from the grave to the throne of the Highest, the man Christ, the God, gloriously ascended.
And yet reflect! In some way, mysterious yet true, he was exalted because he suffered.
“Being found in outward form as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient to death, even the death of the cross.
For this reason God also has highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name.”
Believer, there is comfort for you here, if you will take it.
If Christ was exalted through his degradation, so will you be.
Do not count your steps to triumph by your steps upward, but by those which seem to go downward.
The way to heaven is downhill; he who would be honored forever must sink in his own esteem, and often in that of his fellow men.

Oh! do not think that that fool over there, who is mounting to heaven by his own light opinions of himself and by the flatteries of his fellows, will safely reach Paradise; no, what he rests on will burst, and he will fall and be broken in pieces.
But he who descends into the mines of suffering will find boundless riches there; and he who dives into the depths of grief will find the pearl of everlasting life within its caverns.

Remember, Christian, that you are exalted when you are disgraced; read the slanders of your enemies as the applause of the just; count the scoffing and jeering of wicked men as equal to the praise and honor of the godly; their blame is censure, and their censure praise.

Reckon too, if your body should ever be exposed to persecution, that it is no shame to you, but the reverse; and if you should be privileged (and you may be) to wear the blood-red crown of martyrdom, count it no disgrace to die.
Remember, the most honorable in the church are “the noble army of martyrs.”

Reckon that the greater the sufferings they endured, so much the greater is their “eternal weight of glory”; and so, if you stand in the brunt and thick of the fight, remember that you will stand in the midst of glory.
If you have the hardest to bear, you will have the sweetest to enjoy.
On with you, then—through floods, through fire, through death, through hell, if it should lie in your path.
Do not fear. He who glorified Christ because he stooped will glorify you; for after he has caused you to endure a while, he will give you “a crown of life which does not fade away.”
III. And now, in the last place, beloved, here is yet another comfort for you.
THE PERSON who exalted Christ is to be noticed.
“GOD also has highly exalted him.”
The emperor of all the Russians crowns himself: he is an autocrat, and puts the crown on his own head: but Christ has no such foolish pride.
Christ did not crown himself.
“GOD also has highly exalted him.”

The crown was put on the head of Christ by God; and there is to me a very sweet reflection in this—that the hand that put the crown on Christ’s head will one day put the crown on ours—that the same Mighty One who crowned Christ “King of kings, and Lord of lords,” will crown us, when he makes us “kings and priests to him forever.”
“I know,” said Paul, “there is laid up for me a crown of glory which does not fade away, which God, the righteous judge, will give me on that day.”

Now, just pause over this thought—that Christ did not crown himself, but that his Father crowned him; that he did not raise himself to the throne of majesty, but that his Father lifted him there, and placed him on his throne.
Why, reflect like this: Man never highly exalted Christ.
Then set this against it—“God also has highly exalted him.”
Man hissed at him, mocked him, hooted at him.
Words were not hard enough—they would use stones.
“They took up stones again to stone him.”
And stones failed; nails must be used, and he must be crucified.
And then there comes the taunt, the jeer, the mockery, while he hangs languishing on the cross of death.
Man did not exalt him.
Set the black picture there.
Now put this glorious, this bright scene side by side with it, and the one will be a foil to the other.
Man dishonored him; “God also exalted him.”
Believer, if all men speak ill of you, lift up your head and say, “Man did not exalt my Master; I thank him that he does not exalt me.
The servant should not be above his master, nor the servant above his lord, nor he who is sent greater than he who sent him.”

blocks.x:
“If on my face for his dear name,
Shame and reproach shall be;
I’ll hail reproach and welcome shame,
For he’ll remember me.”

s: God will remember me, and highly exalt me after all, though man casts me down.
Set it, again, against the fact that Christ did not exalt himself.
Poor Christian! you feel that you cannot exalt yourself.
Sometimes you cannot raise your poor depressed spirits.
Some say to you, “Oh! you should not feel like this.”
They tell you, “Oh! you should not speak such words, nor think such thoughts.”
Ah! “the heart knows its own bitterness, and a stranger does not meddle with it”—yes, and I will improve on it, “nor a friend either.”
It is not easy to tell how another ought to feel and how another ought to act.
Our minds are made differently, each in its own mold, which mold is broken afterward, and there will never be another like it.
We are all different, each one of us; but I am sure there is one thing in which we are all brought to unite in times of deep sorrow, namely, in a sense of helplessness.
We feel that we cannot exalt ourselves.
Now remember, our Master felt just like this.
In the 22nd Psalm, which, if I read it rightly, is a beautiful soliloquy of Christ on the cross, he says to himself, “I am a worm, and no man.”
As if he felt himself so broken, so cast down, that instead of being more than a man, as he was, he felt for a while less than a man.

And yet, when he could not lift a finger to crown himself, when he could scarcely summon a thought of victory, when his eye could not flash with even a distant glimpse of triumph—then his God was crowning him.
Are you so broken in pieces, Christian?
Do not think that you are cast away forever; for “God also has highly exalted him” who did not exalt himself; and this is a picture and prophecy of what he will do for you.
And now, beloved, I can say little more on this text, except that I bid you now for a few minutes meditate and think on it.
Oh! let your eyes be lifted up; bid heaven’s blue veil divide; ask power of God—I mean spiritual power from on high—to look within the veil.
I do not bid you look to the streets of gold, nor to the walls of jasper, nor to the pearly-gated city.
I do not ask you to turn your eyes to the white-robed hosts, who forever sing loud hallelujahs; but there, my friends, turn your eyes,
Do you see him?

blocks.x:
“The head that once was crowned with thorns,
Is crowned with glory now;
A royal diadem adorns
That mighty Victor’s brow.

No more the bloody crown,
The cross and nails no more:
For hell itself shakes at his frown,
And all the heavens adore.”

s: Look at him! Can your imagination picture him?
Behold his transcendent glory!
The majesty of kings is swallowed up; the pomp of empires dissolves like the white mist of the morning before the sun; the brightness of assembled armies is eclipsed.
He in himself is brighter than the sun, more terrible than armies with banners.
See him! See him!
O hide your heads, you monarchs; put away your gaudy pageantry, you lords of this poor narrow earth!
His kingdom knows no bounds; without a limit his vast empire stretches itself out.
Above him all is his; beneath him, many a step down, are angels, and they are his; and they cast their crowns before his feet.
With them stand his elect and ransomed, and their crowns too are his.

And here on this lower earth stand his saints, and they are his, and they adore him; and under the earth, among the inhabitants of hell, where devils growl their malice, even there is trembling and adoration; and where lost spirits, with wailing and gnashing of teeth, forever lament their existence, even there, there is the acknowledgment of his Godhead, even though the confession helps to make the fire of their torments.
In heaven, on earth, in hell, all knees bend before him, and every tongue confesses that he is God.
If not now, yet in the time that is to come this shall be carried out, that every creature of God’s making shall acknowledge his Son to be “God over all, blessed forever.
Amen.” Oh! my soul anticipates that blessed day, when this whole earth shall bend its knee before its God willingly!
I do believe there is a happy era coming, when there will not be one knee unbent before my Lord and Master.

I look for that time, that latter-day glory, when kings shall bring presents, when queens shall be the nursing mothers of the church, when the gold of Sheba and the ships of Tarshish and the dromedaries of Arabia shall alike be his, when nations and tribes of every tongue shall

blocks.x:
“Dwell on his name with sweetest song,
And infant voices shall proclaim
Their early blessings on his name.”

s: Sometimes I hope to live to see that most auspicious era—that halcyon age of this world, so much oppressed with grief and sorrow by the tyranny of its own inhabitants.

I hope to see the time when it shall be said, “Shout, for the great Shepherd reigns, and his unsuffering kingdom now is come”—when earth shall be one great orchestra of praise, and every man shall sing the glorious hallelujah anthem of the King of kings.
But even now, while waiting for that era, my soul rejoices in the fact that every knee does virtually bow—though not willingly, yet really.
Does the scoffer, when he mouths at high heaven, think that he insults God?
He thinks so, but his insult dies long before it reaches halfway to the stars.
Does he imagine, when in his malice he forges a sword against Christ, that his weapon will prosper?

If he does, I can well imagine the derision of God, when he sees the wildest rebel, the most abandoned despiser, still working out his great decrees, still doing what God has eternally ordained, and in the midst of his wild rebellion still running in the very track which in some mysterious way before all eternity had been marked out as the track in which that being should certainly move.

“The wild steeds of earth have broken their bridles, the reins are out of the hands of the charioteer”—so some say; but they are not, or if they are, the steeds run the same course as they would have done had the Almighty still grasped the reins.

The world has not gone to confusion; chance is not God; God is still Master, and let men do what they will, and hate the truth we now prize, they will after all do what God wills, and their direst rebellion will prove to be but a kind of obedience, though they do not know it.
But you will say, “Why do you still find fault? For who has resisted such a will as that?”
“No, but O man, who are you that answers back against God?
Shall the thing that is formed say to the one who formed it, Why have you made me this way?
Has the potter not power over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel to honor and another to dishonor?

What if God, willing to display his wrath and to make his power known, bore with much long-suffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction: and that he might make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he had before made ready for glory.”
Who is he that shall blame him?
Woe to the one who strives with his Maker!
He is God—know that, you inhabitants of the land; and all things, after all, shall serve his will.

I like what Luther says in his bold hymn, where, notwithstanding all that those who hate predestination choose to affirm, he knew and boldly declared, “He everywhere has sway, and all things serve his might.”
Notwithstanding all they do, there is God’s sway, after all.
Go on, reviler! God knows how to turn all your revilings into songs!
Go on, you warrior against God, if you will; know this: your sword shall help to magnify God and carve out glory for Christ, when you intended the slaughter of his church.
It shall come to pass that all you do will be frustrated; for God makes the diviners mad, and says, “Where is the wisdom of the scribe?
Where is the wisdom of the wise?”
Surely, “Him God has exalted, and given him a name which is above every name.”

And now, lastly, beloved, if it is true, as it is, that Christ is so exalted that he is to have a name above every name, and every knee is to bow to him, will we not bow our knees this morning before his Majesty?
You must, whether you will or not, one day bow your knee.
O iron-sinewed sinner, bow your knee now!
You will have to bow it, man, on that day when the lightnings are let loose and the thunders roll in wild fury: you will have to bow your knee then.
Oh! bow it now!
“Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled even a little.”
O Lord of hosts! bend the knees of men!
Make us all the willing subjects of your grace, lest afterward we should be the unwilling slaves of your terror, dragged with chains of vengeance down to hell.
O that those who are on earth might now willingly bend their knees, lest in hell it should be fulfilled, “Things under the earth shall bow the knee before him.”
God bless you, my friends; I can say no more than that.
God bless you, for Jesus’ sake! Amen.
“There is a friend that sticks closer than a brother.”—Proverbs 18:24.
Cicero has rightly said, “Friendship is the only thing in the world about whose usefulness all mankind agrees.”
Friendship seems as necessary an element of a comfortable existence in this world as fire or water, or even air itself.

A man may drag out a miserable existence in proud, solitary dignity, but his life is scarcely life; it is nothing but an existence, the tree of life being stripped of the leaves of hope and the fruits of joy.
He who would be happy here must have friends; and he who would be happy hereafter must, above all things, find a friend in the world to come, in the person of God, the Father of his people.

Friendship, however, though very pleasing and exceedingly blessed, has brought men the greatest misery when it has been unworthy and unfaithful; for just in proportion as a good friend is sweet, a false friend is full of bitterness.
“A faithless friend is sharper than a viper’s tooth.”
It is sweet to rest on someone; but oh, how bitter to have that support snap, and to suffer a grievous fall as the result of your confidence!
Faithfulness is an absolute necessity in a true friend; we cannot rejoice in people unless they will stand faithful to us.
Solomon declares that “there is a friend that sticks closer than a brother.”
That friend, I suppose, he never found in the pomp and vanities of the world.
He had tried them all, but he found them empty; he passed through all their joys, but he found them “vanity of vanities.”
Poor Savage spoke from sad experience when he said—

blocks.x:
“You will find the friendship of the world a show!
Mere outward show! It is like the harlot’s tears,
The statesman’s promise, or the false patriot’s zeal,
Full of fair seeming, but delusion all.”

s: And so, for the most part, they are.
The world’s friendship is always brittle.
Trust in it, and you have trusted a robber; rely on it, and you have leaned on a thorn; yes, worse than that, on a spear that will pierce you to the soul with agony.
Yet Solomon says he had found “a friend that sticks closer than a brother.”

Not in the haunts of his unbridled pleasures, nor in the wanderings of his unlimited resources, but in the pavilion of the Most High, the secret dwelling place of God, in the person of Jesus, the Son of God, the Friend of sinners.
It is saying a great thing to affirm that “there is a friend that sticks closer than a brother”; for the love of brothers has produced most valiant deeds.
We have read stories of what brotherhood could do which, we think, could hardly be surpassed in the records of friendship.
Timoleon, with his shield, stood over the body of his slain brother, to defend him from the insults of the enemy.
It was counted a brave deed of brotherhood that he should dare the spears of an army in defense of his brother’s corpse.
And there have been many such instances, in ancient and modern warfare, of the devotion of brothers to one another.

There is a story told of a Highland regiment that lost its way while marching through the Highlands; they were overtaken by one of those terrible storms that sometimes come upon travelers unawares, and, blinded by the snow, they lost their way on the mountains.
Nearly frozen to death, they could continue their march only with difficulty.
One man after another dropped into the snow and disappeared.

There were two brothers, however, by the name of Forsythe; one of them fell flat on the ground and would have lain there to die, but his brother, though barely able to drag his own limbs across the white desert, took him on his back and carried him along; and as others fell one by one, this brave, true-hearted brother carried his loved one on his back, until at last he himself fell down, overcome with fatigue, and died.
His brother, however, had received such warmth from his body that he was able to reach the end of his journey in safety, and so lived.
Here we have an example of one brother sacrificing his life for another.
I hope there are some brothers here who would be prepared to do the same if they should ever be brought into the same difficulty.
It is saying a great thing to declare that “there is a friend that sticks closer than a brother.”

It is putting that friend first of all in the list of loving ones; for surely, next to a mother’s love, there is, and there ought to be, no higher affection in the world than the love of a brother for one born of the same father and dandled on the same knee.
Those who have “grown in beauty side by side, and filled one house with glee,” ought to love one another.
And we think there have been many glorious examples and mighty proofs of the love of brothers.
Yet, says Solomon, “there is a friend that sticks closer than a brother.”
To repeat our assertion, we believe that this friend is the blessed Redeemer, Jesus Christ.

It will be our task this morning, first, to prove the fact that he sticks closer than a brother; then, as briefly as we can, to show you why he sticks closer than a brother; and then to finish by giving you some lessons that may be drawn from the doctrine that Jesus Christ is a faithful Friend.
I. First, then, beloved, we assert that CHRIST IS “A FRIEND THAT STICKS CLOSER THAN A BROTHER.”
And in order to prove this from facts, we appeal to those of you who have had him for a friend.
Will not each of you at once give your verdict that this is neither more nor less than an unexaggerated truth?

He loved you before all worlds; long before the morning star flung its ray across the darkness, before the wing of an angel had beaten the uncharted heavens, before anything of creation had struggled from the womb of nothingness, God, even our God, had set his heart on all his children.
Since that time, has he once swerved, has he once turned aside, once changed?
No; you who have tasted his love and know his grace will bear me witness that he has been a certain friend in uncertain circumstances.

blocks.x:
“He near your side has always stood.
His loving-kindness, oh, how good!”

s: You fell in Adam; did he stop loving you?
No; he became the second Adam to redeem you.
You sinned in practice and brought upon your head the condemnation of God; you deserved his wrath and his utter anger; did he forsake you then? No!

blocks.x:
“He saw you ruined in the fall,
Yet loved you in spite of all.”

s: He sent his minister after you; you despised him; he preached the gospel in your ears; you laughed at him; you broke God’s Sabbath; you despised his Word.
Did he forsake you then? No!

blocks.x:
“Determined to save, he watched over your path,
While, Satan’s blind slave, you played with death.”

s: And at last he arrested you by his grace; he humbled you, he made you penitent, he brought you to his feet, and he forgave you all your sins.
Since then, has he left you?
You have often left him; has he ever left you?
You have had many trials and troubles; has he ever deserted you?
Has he ever turned away his heart and shut up his tender compassion?
No, children of God, it is your solemn duty to say “No,” and to bear witness to his faithfulness.
You have been in severe afflictions and in dangerous circumstances; did your friend desert you then?
Others have been faithless to you; the one who eats bread with you has raised his heel against you; but has Christ ever forsaken you?
Has there ever been a moment when you could go to him and say, “Master, you have betrayed me”?
Could you once, in the blackest hour of your grief, dare to call his faithfulness into question?
Could you dare to say of him, “Lord, you promised what you did not perform”?
Will you not bear witness now, “Not one good thing has failed of all that the Lord God has promised; all has come to pass”?
And do you fear he will yet forsake you?
Ask, then, the bright ones before the throne—“You glorified spirits!
Did Christ forsake you?
You have passed through Jordan’s stream; did he leave you there?
You have been baptized in the black flood of death; did he forsake you there?
You have stood before the throne of God; did he deny you then?”

And they answered, “No; through all the troubles of our life, in all the bitterness of death, in all the agonies of our dying moments, and in all the terrors of God’s judgment, he has been with us, ‘a friend that sticks closer than a brother.’”
Out of all the millions of God’s redeemed, there is not one he has forsaken.
Poor they have been, lowly and distressed, but he has never despised their prayer, never turned aside from doing them good.
He has always been with them.

blocks.x:
“For his mercy will endure,
Ever faithful, ever sure.”

s: But I will not linger any longer, since I cannot prove this to the ungodly, and to the godly it is already proven, for they know it by experience; therefore there is little need for me to do more than simply certify the fact that Christ is a faithful friend—a friend in every hour of need and every time of distress.

blocks.x: II. And now I have to tell you THE REASONS WHY WE MAY DEPEND ON CHRIST AS A FAITHFUL FRIEND.

s: There are some things in himself which make it certain that he will stick close to his people.
1. True friendship can only be formed between true men.
Hearts are the soul of honor.
There can be no lasting friendship between bad men.

Bad men may pretend to love each other, but their friendship is a rope of sand, which will be broken at any convenient moment; but if a man has a sincere heart within him, and is true and noble, then we may confide in him.
Spenser sings in fine old English verse—

blocks.x:
“No, surely that friendship cannot long endure,
However bright and goodly be its style,
That serves an evil cause or an evil end,
For Virtue is the band that binds hearts most sure.”

s: But who can find a stain in the character of Jesus, or who can tarnish his honor?
Has there ever been a spot on his coat of arms?
Has his flag ever been trampled in the dust?
Does he not stand as the true witness in heaven, the faithful and just?
Is it not declared of him that he is God, who cannot lie?
Have we not found him so up to this moment; and may we not, knowing that he is “Holy, holy, holy Lord,” trust him to stick closer to us than a brother?
His goodness is the guarantee of his faithfulness; he cannot fail us.
2. Faithfulness to us about our faults is a certain sign of fidelity in a friend.
You may depend on the man who will tell you of your faults in a kind and considerate manner.
Fawning hypocrites and insidious flatterers are the sweepings and refuse of friendship.
They are nothing but parasites on that noble tree.
But true friends trust you enough to tell you openly of your faults.

Give me for a friend the man who will speak honestly of me to my face; who will not tell first one neighbor and then another, but who will come straight to my house and say, “Sir, I feel there is such-and-such a thing in you, which, as my brother, I must tell you about.”

That man is a true friend; he has proved himself to be so; for we never get any praise for telling people of their faults; we rather risk their dislike; a man will sometimes thank you for it, but he does not often like you any the better.
Praise is a thing we all love.

I met a man the other day who said he was impervious to flattery; I was walking with him at the time, and turning around rather sharply, I said, “At any rate, sir, you seem to have a great gift for flattering yourself, for you are really doing so in saying you are impervious to flattery.”
“You cannot flatter me,” he said.
I replied, “I can, if I care to try; and perhaps I may do so before the day is out.”

I found I could not flatter him directly, so I began by saying what a fine child that was of his; and he drank it in like a precious draught; and when I praised this thing and that thing belonging to him, I could see that he was very easily flattered—not directly, but indirectly.

We are all open to flattery; we like the soothing cordial, only it must not be labeled flattery; for we have a religious horror of flattery if it is called by that name; call it by any other name, and we drink it in, even as the ox drinks in water.
Now, child of God, has Christ ever flattered you?
Has he not told you of your faults quite truly?
Has he not pricked your conscience even about what you thought to gloss over—your little secret sins?
Has he not stirred your conscience to thunder notes of terror in your ears because of your misdeeds?
Well, then, you may trust him, for he shows that faithfulness which makes a man truly trustworthy.
Thus I have pointed out to you that there are reasons in himself for which we may trust him.
3. In the next place, there are some things in his friendship which make us sure of not being deceived when we put our confidence in him.
True friendship must not be of hasty growth.
As quaint old Master Fuller says: “Let friendship creep gently to a height; if it rushes to it, it may soon run itself out of breath.”
It is even so.
I think it was Joanna Baillie who said—

blocks.x:
“Friendship is no plant of hasty growth.
Though planted in esteem’s deep, settled soil,
The gradual tending of kind fellowship
Must bring it to perfection.”

s: In vain you trust the gourd over your head, O Jonah; it will not be of much use to you; it came up in a night, it may wither in a night.

It is the strong, stiff oak, of ages’ growth, that will withstand the tempest; that will both put out its wings to shield you from the sun and afterward find you a shelter in its heart, if necessary, in its gray old age, when its branches tremble in the blast.
Friendship is true when it begins; but we must have a man’s friendship for a long time before we can say of him that he will stick closer than a brother.
And how long has Christ loved you?
That you cannot tell.

When the ages were not yet born, he loved you; when this world was an infant, wrapped in swaddling clothes of mist, he loved you; when the old pyramids had not yet begun to be built, his heart was set on you; and ever since you were born he has had a strong affection for you.
He looked on you in your cradle, and he loved you then; he was betrothed to you when you were an infant only a span long, and he has loved you ever since.
Some of you I see with gray hair, some with heads quite bald with age; he has loved you until now, and will he now forsake you?
Oh no! His friendship is so old that it must last; it has been matured by so many tempests, it has been rooted by so many winds of trouble, that it cannot but endure; it must stand.

Even as the granite peak of the mountain will not be melted, because, unlike the snow, it has braved the blast and borne the heat of the burning sun; it has always stood out, catching in its face every blow from the face of nature, and yet has remained unmoved and unharmed.
It will last, for it has lasted.
But when the elements melt and run away in a stream of dissolving fire, then Christ’s friendship will still exist, for it is of older growth than they.

He must be “a friend that sticks closer than a brother”; for his friendship is a hoary friendship—as white with age as his own head, of which it is said, “His head and his hair are white like snow, as white as wool.”
4. But note, further, that the friendship which will last does not arise in the chambers of mirth, nor is it fed and fattened there.
Young lady, you speak of a dear friend whom you made last night in a ballroom.
Do not, I beg you, misuse the word; he is not a friend if he was gained merely there; friends are better things than those that grow in the hothouse of pleasure.
Friendship is a more lasting plant than those.
You have a friend, have you?
Yes; and he keeps a pair of horses and has a fine household.

Ah! but your best way to prove your friend is to know that he will be your friend when you have not so much as a humble cottage, and when, homeless and without clothing, you are driven to beg your bread.
That is how you would truly test a friend.
Give me a friend who was born in the wintertime, whose cradle was rocked in the storm; he will last.
Our fair-weather friends will flee away from us.
